tagline: A ridge route through hardwood forest, farmland and Delta history
intro: Crowley's Ridge Parkway follows a rolling rise above the flat Mississippi plain, linking the Missouri Bootheel with Helena-West Helena, Arkansas. The ridge is composed primarily of loess, sediment deposited by wind. Arkansas DOT describes hardwood forest, farmland and orchards along the corridor. The Federal Highway Administration lists this National Scenic Byway at 212 miles, allows 5.5 hours for the drive, and highlights its plant communities, wildlife and historical sites. Its southern forest section winds along a narrow two-lane road past Storm Creek Lake.

Travel along the ridge was easier than travel through the swampy lowlands, making it a north-south communications link. The modern parkway assembled existing roads into a scenic corridor. Within Arkansas, that designation brought together segments of 17 highways, two county roads and several city streets under the parkway name. Arkansas designated its 198-mile portion in 1997; national recognition followed in 1998. An extension into Missouri followed in 2000.

Drive south from the northern end at Malden into Arkansas, through Paragould and Jonesboro toward Forrest City and Marianna. Beyond Marianna, the road passes Bear Creek Lake and Storm Creek Lake in the St. Francis National Forest before reaching West Helena and Helena. The southern end meets US 49 near the Helena Bridge over the Mississippi River.

moments.title: Crowley's Ridge State Park
moments.text: The parkway cuts through Crowley's Ridge State Park, where original stone and log structures survive from the Civilian Conservation Corps' work in the 1930s. The park occupies 291 acres on top of the ridge in Greene County. The site was Benjamin Crowley's homesite before it became a state park in 1933 to honor him and the area's heritage. The bathhouse, bridge, comfort station and dining hall have separate National Register listings. The water has a construction story too: the Arkansas National Guard originally built the 31-acre fishing lake. A second, three-acre lake is spring-fed.

moments.title: Parkin Archeological State Park
moments.text: At the meeting of the St. Francis and Tyronza rivers, a village enclosed by a defensive palisade occupied this site around 1350–1650 CE. One large mound and six smaller mounds were arranged beside a central plaza. The largest mound stood beside the St. Francis River, with the plaza on its other side. Houses followed the alignment of the mound and plaza. Women managed most cultivation and processing of food crops, including developing varieties of maize and vegetables. Potters built vessels from strips of clay, then smoothed them into shape. Artifacts from the site are displayed in its museum.

moments.title: Helena
moments.text: A flour sponsor helped put Helena blues on the radio in 1941. KFFA offered a group of blues musicians an hour on the air if they found a sponsor; King Biscuit Flour agreed. The company sponsored the King Biscuit Entertainers and the show King Biscuit Time. During the 1940s and 1950s, Black people came to Helena from rural Arkansas and the Mississippi Delta for work, and some worked full-time as musicians. Juke joints employed pianists including Sunnyland Slim, Memphis Slim and Roosevelt Sykes. The Delta Cultural Center in downtown Helena tells the regional story, particularly the history of the blues.
